title: Origins of Nationalism
description: Anderson, Gellner, Hobsbawm — imagined communities and modernist accounts

concepts.title: What Nationalism Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Nationalism is the political principle that the nation should be the primary unit of political loyalty, and that the boundaries of the political unit should match the boundaries of the nation. The principle is so central to contemporary political life that it can be hard to see as a specific ideology with specific historical origins; for most of human history, most of humanity organised political loyalty around dynasties, religious communities, city-states, or empires rather than nations.

The dominant scholarly tradition — the 'modernist' school — argues that nationalism is a relatively recent phenomenon, dating from roughly the late 18th century. Its origins are typically located in the French and American revolutions, the consolidation of vernacular print cultures, the breakdown of dynastic legitimacy, and the spread of literacy associated with industrialisation. The 'primordialist' alternative — that nations are deep, organic features of human history reaching back into antiquity — has been substantially marginalised in academic scholarship, though it remains politically influential.

The major modernist theorists — Ernest Gellner, Benedict Anderson, Eric Hobsbawm, Anthony D. Smith (a partial qualification of the modernist position), Liah Greenfeld, and others — disagree about specific mechanisms but agree that nationalism is a feature of modernity rather than a primordial fact about human social organisation. The case is empirical and partly persuasive: the universality of the nation-state form is itself the result of the post-1945 international system of mutual recognition, which extended the nation-state model worldwide in less than a century.

concepts.title: Anderson and Imagined Communities
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential single theoretical framework is Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism (1983, expanded 1991, 2006). Anderson defines the nation as 'an imagined political community — and imagined as both inherently limited and sovereign.' The community is imagined because most members will never know each other but nonetheless share a sense of common identity; limited because every nation has finite boundaries beyond which other nations exist; sovereign because nations claim political self-determination.

Anderson's distinctive contribution is his account of how imagined community became possible at the scale of the nation. The crucial enabling conditions, on his analysis, were: print capitalism (the standardisation of vernacular languages through commercial print, replacing the Latin and dynastic-language hierarchies of medieval Europe); the simultaneous experience of reading the daily newspaper (millions of unrelated people reading the same news at the same hour, imagining themselves as part of a shared time and space); and the secular reorganisation of political legitimacy after the breakdown of dynastic and religious authority.

The model has been criticised in detail. Its emphasis on print capitalism may overstate that mechanism's role compared to, say, mass schooling and military conscription. The Latin American originals of nationalism Anderson emphasises are less centrally important to subsequent European cases than his framing suggests. The general framework has nonetheless been enormously influential, providing the standard vocabulary for thinking about nations as imagined communities — communities that are real, durable, and politically consequential precisely because they are imagined into being through specific cultural and material practices.

concepts.title: Gellner, Hobsbawm, and Industrial Modernity
concepts.contentHtml:
The other major modernist accounts emphasise different but complementary mechanisms. Ernest Gellner's Nations and Nationalism (1983) argued that nationalism is a functional consequence of industrial modernity. Industrial economies require workers who can communicate across the country in a shared standardised language — the agrarian world's localised dialects and stratified literacies don't work for industrial production. Mass schooling teaches the standardised national language and culture; the modern state's bureaucracy operates in that language; the resulting cultural homogenisation is what we call nationalism. On Gellner's analysis, nations follow from industrial modernity rather than the other way around.

Eric Hobsbawm's Nations and Nationalism since 1780 (1990, with The Invention of Tradition, 1983, edited with Terence Ranger) emphasised the constructed character of national traditions. Many of the seemingly-ancient national traditions of European nations — Scottish kilts, German fairy-tale folklore, English coronation rites, the standardised ceremonies of constitutional monarchies — were largely invented or substantially elaborated in the 19th and early 20th centuries to provide nation-building states with the symbolic resources they needed. The 'invention of tradition' framework has been one of the most generative tools for analysing how national consciousness is built rather than discovered.

The contemporary applications are extensive. The post-1989 reconstruction of national identities in former Communist states, the post-2010 rise of explicit ethnic-nationalist parties across Europe, the contestation of 'national history' in many postcolonial states, and the contemporary debates over museum exhibitions, public statues, and curriculum content all illustrate how the modernist analysis of nationalism remains immediately relevant. Nations are not natural; they are made; and the question of who gets to make them and how is one of the most persistently consequential political questions in contemporary politics.

title: Civic vs Ethnic Nationalism
description: Two ideal types of national belonging — and why the line is always blurred

concepts.title: The Two Ideal Types
concepts.contentHtml:
The most-cited typology in nationalism studies distinguishes civic from ethnic nationalism. The distinction was systematised by Hans Kohn in The Idea of Nationalism (1944) and has been refined by subsequent scholars including Liah Greenfeld, Rogers Brubaker, and Bernard Yack. The basic contrast: civic nationalism grounds national membership in shared citizenship, political values, and adherence to common institutions; ethnic nationalism grounds national membership in shared descent, language, religion, or culture.

The civic-nationalist ideal type is typically illustrated by the United States and France. American national identity, in this framing, is grounded in commitment to constitutional principles, democratic institutions, and a creedal liberal-democratic ideology that any immigrant can in principle adopt. French national identity, in the Republican tradition, is grounded in adherence to the values of liberté, égalité, fraternité and the secular Republican constitutional order. Membership is in principle open to any person willing to commit to the political principles that constitute the nation.

The ethnic-nationalist ideal type is typically illustrated by Germany (until the 1999 reform of citizenship law) and many Eastern European cases. German national identity, on this analysis, was traditionally grounded in shared descent — German citizenship was passed through bloodline (jus sanguinis) rather than birthplace, and ethnic Germans from Eastern Europe could claim citizenship even without ever having lived in Germany. Most contemporary cases of explicit ethnic nationalism in Europe — Hungary's Orbán, Poland's pre-2023 PiS, the various far-right parties — operate within this lineage.

concepts.title: Why the Distinction Is Always Blurred
concepts.contentHtml:
The civic-ethnic distinction is more a heuristic than a clean dichotomy. Critical scholarship — particularly Bernard Yack's Nationalism and the Moral Psychology of Community (2012) — has argued that even ostensibly-civic nationalisms have substantial ethnic and cultural content. American civic nationalism has historically excluded various groups (Native Americans, African Americans, women, certain immigrant categories) on grounds that were ultimately ethnic or cultural; the civic ideal has been a regulative ideal more than an accomplished reality.

The French case illustrates the complication well. The French Republican tradition explicitly rejects ethnic categorisation — official statistics do not record race or ethnicity, and the laïc tradition treats all citizens as equally French regardless of background. But the lived experience of French citizens of North African or sub-Saharan African descent, the persistent residential and occupational segregation, the recurring controversies over hijab and Muslim integration suggest that civic universalism has not in practice produced the level of integration the doctrine implies.

The contemporary debate over national identity in many democracies — the British debate over what constitutes 'Britishness,' the American debate over civic versus ethnic-cultural national identity, the European debates over Muslim integration — operates partly along the civic-ethnic axis but also along orthogonal dimensions (multicultural vs assimilationist, religious vs secular, individual vs group rights). The categories remain useful but can mask substantial heterogeneity in actual cases. The contemporary right-populist movement in many democracies has explicitly mobilised against civic-universalist national-identity conceptions, often without explicitly endorsing the ethnic-nationalist alternative — a position that the civic-ethnic typology does not handle well.

concepts.title: Multiculturalism and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-1945 expansion of immigration in advanced democracies forced renewed thinking about how national identity should accommodate cultural diversity. The multiculturalism framework — most fully developed in Canadian and Australian policy through the 1970s and 1980s — held that ethnic and cultural minorities should have positive rights to maintain their distinctive cultures alongside common citizenship. The Canadian Multiculturalism Act of 1988 was one of the most ambitious legal expressions of the framework.

The critique of multiculturalism has come from multiple directions. Liberal individualists (Brian Barry's Culture and Equality, 2001) argue that multicultural-group rights conflict with individual rights, particularly for women and dissenters within minority communities. Civic-nationalist critics argue that multiculturalism undermines the shared national identity that holds democracies together. Empirical critics point to apparent failures of multicultural policy — the persistence of inter-group inequality, the perceived lack of integration of some Muslim communities in Europe, the post-9/11 security concerns — as evidence that the framework has not delivered on its promises.

The defence of multiculturalism has come from Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995), Charles Taylor (The Politics of Recognition, 1992), and others. Kymlicka argues that liberal individualist principles actually require recognition of group rights for many minority cultures, because individuals can only flourish within meaningful cultural contexts. Taylor emphasises the importance of recognition itself — being acknowledged as a member of a respected cultural community — for individual identity. The debate continues to inform contemporary policy in many democracies. The pendulum has swung partly toward more assimilationist approaches in the 2010s and 2020s, but the underlying questions — how should liberal democracies handle cultural diversity, what kinds of group rights are appropriate, what kinds of common identity are necessary for democratic stability — remain unresolved.

title: Self-Determination & Secession
description: From Wilson to Catalonia — the politics of nation-building and breakup

concepts.title: Wilson and the Self-Determination Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
The principle of national self-determination — that nations have the right to choose their political status, particularly the right to form independent states — became central to international politics through the post-1918 settlement. President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) and his subsequent advocacy at the Paris Peace Conference made self-determination a guiding principle for redrawing the European map after the collapse of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian empires.

The Versailles settlement (1919) and associated treaties produced new states — Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, the Baltic states, an attempted Armenian state — substantially organised on national-self-determination principles. The settlement was famously imperfect: borders included substantial minorities (German speakers in Czechoslovakia and Poland, Hungarians in Romania and Yugoslavia, etc.); some self-determination claims (Kurdish, Palestinian, much of the post-Ottoman Arab world) were ignored or postponed; and the resulting international order was structurally unstable in ways that contributed to the rise of inter-war revisionism and the Second World War.

The post-1945 expansion of self-determination principles through the UN Charter and subsequent decolonisation transformed the doctrine from primarily-European concern to a global principle of international law. The 1960 UN Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries codified the right of self-determination for colonised peoples. The legal application has been more complicated than the rhetoric: self-determination has typically been understood to permit the conversion of existing colonial units into independent states, not to permit secession from established states. The persistent tension between the right of self-determination and the principle of territorial integrity remains unresolved.

concepts.title: Secession in International Law
concepts.contentHtml:
The legal status of secession in international law is one of the most contested areas of contemporary jurisprudence. The general principle is that international law neither prohibits nor explicitly endorses secession; the question is whether new states emerge by accepted procedures and gain international recognition. The 1991 dissolution of the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia produced multiple new states recognised through somewhat different legal frameworks; the 2008 Kosovo independence declaration produced a sustained recognition dispute that remains substantially unresolved (over 100 states recognise Kosovo; Russia, China, and several others do not).

The Quebec case provides one of the clearest legal precedents. The Canadian Supreme Court's 1998 Reference re Secession of Quebec ruling held that Quebec did not have a unilateral right to secede under either Canadian or international law, but that a clear majority of Quebecers expressing a clear preference for secession would impose a constitutional obligation on Canada to negotiate in good faith over the terms of separation. The decision has been influential as a model for how to handle secession claims through institutional processes rather than unilateral declarations.

The Catalan case (2017) and the Scottish case (2014, with continued debate since) illustrate contrasting approaches. Spain treated the Catalan independence referendum as illegal under the Spanish constitution and prosecuted its organisers; the UK negotiated the 2014 Scottish referendum through a constitutional agreement that legitimised a binary in/out vote. The two responses produced very different outcomes despite roughly comparable underlying nationalist movements. The pattern illustrates how secession outcomes depend less on the legal merits of the case than on the institutional response of the state from which secession is sought.

concepts.title: When Self-Determination Conflicts with Itself
concepts.contentHtml:
The hardest cases of self-determination involve situations where the principle generates competing claims that cannot all be satisfied. Israel-Palestine is the canonical case: both Israeli Jews and Palestinian Arabs have plausible self-determination claims to the same territory; any settlement requires compromising at least one of those claims. How far the recurring failure of two-state negotiations reflects this structural difficulty, and how far particular leaders' choices, is itself fiercely contested.

The Russian-Ukrainian conflict raises similar questions in a different form. Russian justifications for the post-2014 interventions and the 2022 full-scale invasion have invoked self-determination claims for Russian-speaking populations in eastern Ukraine. The Ukrainian counter-claim is that internal minority rights are appropriately handled within the Ukrainian state and that armed external intervention to support secession violates international law. The international response — overwhelming support for Ukraine, sanctions on Russia, ICJ proceedings — has reflected the latter view, but the underlying conceptual question of when external intervention to support self-determination is legitimate remains genuinely contested.

The Kurdish case spans four states (Turkey, Iraq, Iran, Syria) with substantially different national-policy responses. The Iraqi Kurdish region has substantial autonomy; the Syrian Kurdish areas (Rojava) achieved de facto autonomy during the Syrian civil war but remain under threat; Turkish Kurdish nationalism has been violently suppressed; Iranian Kurdish areas are subject to ongoing repression. The case illustrates how the same self-determination claim can produce very different outcomes depending on the receiving state's political choices and capabilities. The principle of self-determination, despite its central role in international rhetoric, does not produce determinate answers in hard cases — and the hard cases are most of the consequential ones.

title: Identity Politics
description: Race, gender, sexuality — recognition and redistribution in modern democracies

concepts.title: What Identity Politics Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Identity politics is the broad family of political mobilisations organised around shared social identity — race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, religion, disability, and various other categories — rather than around the class-and-economic-interest categories that dominated 20th-century political mobilisation. The term has both descriptive and pejorative uses; in academic political theory it is largely descriptive, while in political commentary it is often deployed as a critical label.

The intellectual roots of contemporary identity politics include several distinct traditions. The American civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s established the political viability of mass mobilisation around racial identity for the purpose of legal equality. Second-wave feminism in the 1960s and 1970s organised around gendered experiences of inequality. Gay liberation after Stonewall (1969) developed the political organisation of sexual identities. Black Power articulated more confrontational and identity-affirming variants of racial mobilisation. The 1977 Combahee River Collective Statement, written by Black feminists, articulated the foundational framework for what came to be called intersectional identity politics — the recognition that multiple identity categories interact in shaping political experience.

The theoretical elaboration of identity politics has been substantial. Iris Marion Young's Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990) argued that genuine social justice requires attention to oppression that operates along identity lines, not just resource distribution. Charles Taylor's 'The Politics of Recognition' (1992) argued for the political importance of recognition itself. Kimberlé Crenshaw's 1989 introduction of the term 'intersectionality' provided the standard vocabulary for analysing how multiple identity categories interact. The combined intellectual tradition has produced one of the most influential frameworks in contemporary political theory.

concepts.title: Recognition and Redistribution
concepts.contentHtml:
The most useful single conceptual distinction in thinking about identity politics is Nancy Fraser's contrast between recognition and redistribution, developed in Justice Interruptus (1997) and her debate with Axel Honneth (Redistribution or Recognition?, 2003). Some political claims concern economic inequality — wages, wealth, capital ownership — and require redistributive responses. Other claims concern cultural injustice — disrespect, misrepresentation, denial of equal moral status — and require recognition. Most actual political mobilisations involve both dimensions in combination, but the conceptual distinction matters because the appropriate institutional responses differ.

Fraser's argument is that contemporary politics has shifted disproportionately toward recognition and away from redistribution, with consequences for the kinds of inequalities that get political attention. The intellectual case is that recognition struggles produce institutional changes (anti-discrimination law, multicultural-curriculum reforms, hate-speech rules) that may be valuable in their own right but that do not address the structural-economic inequalities that often correlate with identity-based marginalisation. The empirical case for this argument is contested but has been influential in continuing left-wing debates about the relationship between identity and class politics.

The contemporary critiques of identity politics have come from multiple directions. The traditional left critique (from Adolph Reed, Walter Benn Michaels, others) argues that identity politics distracts from class organising. The liberal critique (Mark Lilla, Francis Fukuyama) argues that fragmentation of political identity into proliferating identity categories undermines the shared civic identity democracies need. The conservative critique argues that identity politics promotes resentment and fragmentation. The defenders of identity politics respond that the alternatives — ignoring identity-based oppression in favour of putatively-universal politics — historically excluded the very groups identity politics seeks to mobilise.

concepts.title: The Contemporary Politics of Recognition
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2010 period has seen a substantial intensification of identity-based political contestation in many democracies. The Black Lives Matter movement in the US (founded 2013, intensified after 2014 Ferguson and 2020 Floyd protests) became one of the largest political movements in US history. The #MeToo movement (2017) reshaped legal and cultural responses to sexual harassment and assault. The expansion of LGBTQ+ rights — same-sex marriage in over 30 countries, the increasing visibility of trans and non-binary identities, the related backlash — has been one of the most rapid post-1945 social transformations. The indigenous rights movement in settler-colonial states (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the US) has produced substantial institutional changes.

The backlash to expanded identity politics has been one of the central political forces of the 2010s and 2020s. The post-2016 right-populist movements in many countries have explicitly mobilised against perceived 'woke' or 'identity politics' overreach. State-level legislation in the US (Florida's 'Don't Say Gay' law, the Stop WOKE Act, anti-trans sports and healthcare legislation) and parallel measures in Hungary, Russia, and elsewhere illustrate the legislative side of the backlash. Whether the post-2024 US administration's efforts to roll back identity-related policy reflect the durable political coalition or a temporary reaction is one of the central political questions of the period.

The theoretical question of how to do identity politics well — recognising the genuine importance of identity-based oppression without producing the fragmentation and resentment its critics identify — remains unsettled. The recent work of Olufemi Taiwo (Elite Capture, 2022), Adolph Reed, Yascha Mounk, and others continues to debate how the concerns of identity politics should be integrated with broader political programmes. The honest assessment is that this is one of the genuinely difficult questions in contemporary political theory, with reasonable people disagreeing on substantive grounds rather than purely on partisan ones.

title: Populism
description: Mudde, Müller — the people vs the elite, on left and right

concepts.title: Defining Populism
concepts.contentHtml:
The contemporary academic consensus on populism derives largely from Cas Mudde's Populism in Europe and the Americas (2012, with Cristóbal Rovira Kaltwasser) and Jan-Werner Müller's What Is Populism? (2016). Mudde's 'thin ideology' definition: populism is a thin-centred ideology that considers society to be ultimately separated into two homogeneous and antagonistic groups — 'the pure people' versus 'the corrupt elite' — and which argues that politics should be an expression of the volonté générale (general will) of the people.

The 'thin' label is important. Populism is not a complete political programme; it can attach itself to left-wing or right-wing substantive content. Left-populism — represented by Hugo Chávez and the Bolivarian movement, Spain's Podemos in its early form, parts of Bernie Sanders's US movement, the post-2010 Latin American left more broadly — combines populism with redistributive economics and (sometimes) ethnic-inclusive politics. Right-populism — represented by Donald Trump, Marine Le Pen, Viktor Orbán, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Narendra Modi, Jair Bolsonaro, Giorgia Meloni — combines populism with cultural conservatism, often nationalism, and (in many cases) opposition to immigration.

Müller's parallel definition emphasises a key feature: populists claim that they alone represent the 'real people' and that their political opponents are illegitimate by definition. The claim is non-pluralistic — populists do not merely disagree with their opponents about policy; they deny the legitimacy of their opponents' standing in the political community. This anti-pluralist feature distinguishes populism from ordinary democratic competition and explains why populist governance, even in formally democratic frameworks, tends toward majoritarian erosion of constitutional protections, judicial independence, and minority rights.

concepts.title: Why Populism Has Risen
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2008 surge of populist movements in many democracies has been one of the central political phenomena of the past fifteen years. Multiple causal mechanisms have been proposed and the empirical literature is unsettled, but several factors recur in explanations.

The economic account emphasises the post-2008 financial crisis, the perceived failure of 'establishment' politics to address its consequences, and the longer trajectory of working-class economic stagnation in advanced economies. The 'left-behind' regions of advanced democracies — deindustrialised areas, former mining and manufacturing zones, depressed agricultural regions — have voted disproportionately for populist parties. The cultural account emphasises immigration, demographic change, and the perceived liberal-cosmopolitan homogenisation of national elites. Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart's Cultural Backlash (2019) argues that the cultural dimension is more important than the economic, with right-populism in particular driven by 'silent counter-revolution' against post-1960s cultural change.

The institutional account emphasises features of democratic political competition that have made populism electorally viable: the decline of mass political parties; the rise of personalised media and social-media-driven mobilisation; the breakdown of post-1945 political-class consensus on issues including European integration, immigration, and economic management. The three accounts are not mutually exclusive — most actual populist movements have economic, cultural, and institutional dimensions in combination. The empirical balance among them varies by country and by period; the disagreement among scholars about the relative weights reflects the genuine complexity of the phenomenon.

concepts.title: Populism in Power and Democratic Backsliding
concepts.contentHtml:
The most consequential empirical finding from a decade of populist governance is that populism in power tends toward democratic backsliding — the erosion of constitutional, judicial, and media protections that distinguish democracies from competitive-authoritarian regimes. Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt's How Democracies Die (2018) and the broader 'democratic backsliding' literature have documented the recurring pattern. Hungary's Orbán has been the most-studied case; the post-2010 Hungarian transformation produced a competitive-authoritarian regime within a formally democratic framework. Poland's PiS government from 2015 to 2023 followed a partial version of the same playbook; the 2023 electoral loss was a partial check on the pattern.

The American case is contested. The post-2016 stress on US constitutional norms — pressure on the Department of Justice, refusal of peaceful transfer of power, the January 6 2021 Capitol attack, the post-2024 administrative-state restructuring — has been interpreted by many democratic-resilience scholars as a populist-driven backsliding pattern parallel to the Hungarian and Polish cases. The defenders of the post-2024 administration argue that the institutional changes are within constitutional limits and that the threat to democracy is overstated. The next several years will provide more evidence.

The responses to populism have been varied and partly unsatisfying. Constitutional protections (judicial review, federal structures, supermajority requirements) have helped slow but not always stopped backsliding. Civil-society mobilisation has produced electoral defeats of populist movements in some cases (Brazil 2022, Poland 2023, Hungary 2026) but not others. The international response — EU rule-of-law conditionality, the Council of Europe, Magnitsky sanctions — has been imperfect but partially effective. Whether democracies have built the institutional resilience to handle sustained populist challenges through multiple electoral cycles is one of the central political questions of the contemporary period.

title: Religion & Politics
description: Secularism, theocracy, religious nationalism — sacred and political authority

concepts.title: Models of Religion-State Relations
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern democracies handle religion-state relations through several distinct models. Strict separation — the United States' First Amendment Establishment Clause, France's laïcité codified in the 1905 Law of Separation, Mexico's post-revolutionary constitutional tradition — formally bars the state from supporting any religion. Established religion — the Church of England in England, the Lutheran national churches of Scandinavia until recent reforms, the Greek Orthodox Church in Greece — gives one religion formal state recognition while typically protecting religious minorities. Pluralist accommodation — Germany's recognised religious bodies (Körperschaften des öffentlichen Rechts), the Netherlands' historical pillarisation, India's complex personal-law system — recognises multiple religions in differentiated institutional arrangements.

The French model of laïcité is one of the most distinctive. The 1905 Law of Separation established strong state neutrality on religious questions; the 2004 prohibition of conspicuous religious symbols in public schools, the 2010 ban on full-face veils in public spaces, and subsequent measures have made laïcité one of the more interventionist forms of secularism in advanced democracies. Critics argue that French secularism has effectively become a particular kind of cultural-majority politics rather than genuine neutrality; defenders argue it is essential to maintaining a shared civic space across religious differences.

The American model of First Amendment separation has produced a different equilibrium. Strong protection for free religious exercise (the Free Exercise Clause), strong protection against establishment, and a complex jurisprudence around government funding, religious symbols in public spaces, and religious accommodation. The post-2020 Supreme Court has shifted the balance somewhat, with cases like Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) and Carson v. Makin (2022) reducing some of the establishment-clause restrictions on government interaction with religion. Whether the US model produces a more workable accommodation than the French one is contested; the empirical evidence on religious-minority integration is mixed across the comparison.

concepts.title: Religious Nationalism
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most important post-1990 political developments has been the rise of explicitly religious nationalism — political movements that ground national identity in religious tradition and use state power to advance religiously-defined goals. The category includes: Hindu nationalism (the BJP, RSS, and broader Sangh Parivar in India); Christian nationalism (Russia's Russian Orthodox-aligned Putinism, Hungary's Orbán-Fidesz, the post-2016 American Christian-nationalist movement); Buddhist nationalism (Myanmar's Ma Ba Tha, Sri Lanka's BBS); Islamic political movements (Iran's Islamic Republic, Erdoğan's AKP-era Turkey, the various Salafist political movements).

The Indian case is particularly important. The BJP's 2014 and 2019 election victories and its 2024 narrowed third-term victory have produced the most successful single example of post-Cold-War religious-nationalist governance in a major democracy. The BJP government has implemented the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019, controversial for differential treatment of Muslim refugees), revoked Article 370 (2019, ending Kashmir's special status), prosecuted opposition figures and journalists at a sustained rate, and built the Ram Mandir at Ayodhya (2024) on the site of the demolished Babri Masjid. The combination of formal democracy with explicitly Hindu-nationalist content has been one of the central comparative-democracy questions of the period.

The Iranian case illustrates a different pattern: explicit theocratic rule with formally democratic elements (an elected parliament and president, but operating under the Supreme Leader's authority and with candidate vetting by the Guardian Council). The 1979 Islamic Revolution produced a regime that has lasted longer than most observers initially expected, with substantial internal opposition (the 2009 Green Movement, the 2022 Mahsa Amini protests) but durable institutional continuity. The model has had limited international imitators despite Iranian state efforts to promote it.

concepts.title: Secularisation, Its Limits, and Contemporary Trends
concepts.contentHtml:
The mid-20th-century social-science consensus assumed a strong secularisation thesis: that economic development, urbanisation, and education would progressively reduce religious belief and political role of religion. The data through the late 20th century broadly supported the thesis in advanced economies — the secularisation of Western Europe is one of the most extensively documented social transformations of the post-war period. The thesis was substantially overturned by the late 20th century's evidence: the United States remained much more religious than the secularisation thesis predicted; the post-1979 Islamic revival across the Muslim world; the post-1980 evangelical and Pentecostal expansion in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa; the rise of Hindu and Buddhist nationalism; the post-2000 migration-driven changes in European religious demographics.

The contemporary religious landscape is more varied than either secularisation or counter-secularisation hypotheses predict. Pew Research Center's sustained measurement programme has documented that religious affiliation continues to grow in absolute terms globally but is becoming concentrated in particular regions (sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Asia) while declining in others (most of Europe, increasingly the US). The category of 'nones' — those without formal religious affiliation — has grown rapidly in many advanced democracies, representing one of the largest religious-identity changes since the Reformation.

The contemporary politics of religion remain intensely consequential. The post-2014 Russian invocation of Orthodox Christianity in geopolitical positioning; the contestation of Christian and Hindu nationalism in Western and Asian democracies; the recurring contestation of religious-versus-secular education, abortion law, LGBTQ+ rights, and other policy areas where religious and secular constituencies disagree; the role of religious leaders in democratic politics — none of these has been resolved by the broader secularising trends. Whether liberal-democratic frameworks can accommodate sustained religious-political mobilisation, both for and against, is one of the central institutional questions of the contemporary period — and the answer varies substantially across countries with different historical traditions of church-state relations.
